newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: Slovenian Foreign Minister quits after criticism.
newsitem.headline: Slovenian Foreign Minister quits after criticism.

text.p: Slovenian Foreign Minister Zoran Thaler resigned on Thursday amid growing pressure from opposition parties who blame him for forcing the country to change its constitution and failing to win entry to NATO.

Thaler, 35, said in a statement that he had resigned due to growing political differences in the country and he wanted to ensure national unity at a time when Slovenia was preparing to integrate into Europe.
"With my resignation, I want to draw attention to the need for national unity in order to place Slovenia in the safe and developed part of Europe," he said.

Thaler is a member of Prime Minister Janez Drnovsek's centre-left Liberal Democrats and has been serving as foreign minister since February when a new government was formed following an inconclusive general election in November.

It is the second time Thaler has lost his job as foreign minister. He was forced out of office in a parliamentary confidence vote in May 1996 after being accused of botching Slovenia's bid for associate membership of the European Union.
The accord was finally signed in June 1996.
Thaler had come under pressure this time from the opposition centre-right Social Democrats, who have called for a parliamentary debate on the coalition government's performance.
The debate, which is expected to take place in September, could lead to a no-confidence vote in the government, which has a majority of eight in the 90-seat parliament.

The Social Democrats have blamed Thaler for being partly responsible for Slovenia having to change its constitution to allow foreigners to buy land in accordance with its associate accord with the EU.

The Social Democrats and opposition Christian Democrats have also accused Thaler of failing to win the backing of NATO states to be included in the first wave of ex-communist states to join the 16-member military alliance.
NATO agreed at a summit in Madrid earlier this month to invite only the Czech Republic, Hungary and Poland to join the alliance. Slovenia and Romania are to be considered at a later date.
